stories.title: The Man in the Dark Room

pages.text: In Cairo, about a thousand years ago, a boy called Yusuf worked for a baker near the great mosque of Al-Azhar. Every morning, he carried warm bread to a house at the end of a narrow street. People in the market said that the man inside was very strange. "He sits in the dark all day," the baker warned him. "Leave the bread at the door, and don't ask him any questions."

One morning, the door was open, and Yusuf heard a calm voice from inside. "Come in, young man, but close the door quickly!" The room was completely dark except for one tiny hole in the wooden shutter of the window. Yusuf's heart was beating fast, but he was curious, so he stepped inside.

Then he noticed something amazing on the white wall. He could see the street outside, with all its colours and people moving! But everything was upside down. A camel was walking slowly across the wall with its feet in the air. "Is this magic?" Yusuf whispered.

The man laughed kindly. "No, it isn't magic. It's light. My name is Al-Hasan Ibn al-Haytham, and I have been studying light for many years." He explained that light travels in straight lines, so the light from the camel's head passes through the hole and lands at the bottom of the wall. "Never believe something just because a famous book says it," he added. "Test it with your own eyes."

After that day, Yusuf visited the scholar whenever he had free time. Ibn al-Haytham did experiments with candles, mirrors and bowls of water, and he wrote down every result carefully. In those days, many people believed that our eyes send out rays so that we can see. "If that were true, we could see in the dark," Ibn al-Haytham said. "Light comes into our eyes from the world, not the other way round."

One windy evening, while Ibn al-Haytham was praying at the mosque, a candle fell onto a pile of his papers. Yusuf was sweeping the floor when he smelled smoke. Without stopping to think, he grabbed a bowl of water and threw it over the flames. His hand was slightly burned, but most of the pages were safe.

When the scholar came back, he stared at the wet, black edges of his papers for a long time. "These pages are ten years of my life," he said quietly. "You have saved them, Yusuf." From then on, he taught the boy to write neatly, and Yusuf helped him to copy his great work, the Book of Optics.

Many years later, the book was translated into other languages and studied by scholars for hundreds of years. Even today, cameras work in the same way as that dark room in Cairo. Yusuf, now an old man with grandchildren, often told them, "I knew him. He taught me to ask questions." And whenever Yusuf saw sunlight shining through a small hole, he smiled.

questions.q: What was Yusuf's job at the start of the story?
options: He carried bread for a baker.
He sold camels in the market.
He cleaned the mosque.

questions.q: Why did the camel look upside down on the wall?
options: Because the wall was broken.
Because light travels in straight lines through the hole.
Because Yusuf was standing on his head.

questions.q: In the story, what does the word "curious" mean?
options: Very afraid of something
Wanting to know or learn about something
Tired and sleepy

questions.q: How did Yusuf save the papers?
options: He called the baker for help.
He carried the papers outside.
He threw a bowl of water over the fire.

questions.q: What was the most important lesson Ibn al-Haytham taught Yusuf?
options: To test ideas and ask questions himself
To always believe famous books
To stay away from dark rooms

pages.text: Every afternoon after school, Faisal climbed the stairs to the roof of his family's house in Riyadh. There, next to his mother's plants, stood his homemade weather station: a thermometer, a small wind vane and an old barometer that his uncle had given him. He wrote every number carefully in a blue notebook. "One day, I'm going to be a real meteorologist," he often told his little sister, Noura.

On Thursday evening, Father announced some exciting news. "Tomorrow we're going to the desert with Grandfather and your cousins," he said. "We'll set up the tent, cook dinner and watch the stars." Faisal checked the weather forecast on his tablet, and it said: sunny, light winds, no rain.

The next afternoon, the camp was full of noise and laughter. The boys were playing football on the red sand while Grandfather made coffee over the fire. But Faisal had brought his barometer, and when he looked at it, he frowned. The pressure was falling fast, faster than he had ever seen before.

"I think the weather is going to change," Faisal told his cousin Saad. Saad laughed and pointed at the sky, which didn't have a single cloud in it. "Your little machine is broken, Faisal!" But Faisal noticed that the birds had disappeared, and the hot air felt strangely heavy and still.

Faisal ran to Grandfather, who was sitting quietly by the fire. The old man listened, then stood up and looked towards the west for a long time. Far away, a thin brown line was growing along the horizon. "The boy is right," Grandfather said calmly. "A sandstorm is coming, so we must leave now."

Everyone packed as quickly as they could, and within ten minutes the cars were moving towards the main road. Through the back window, Faisal watched a huge wall of dust rise into the sky, as tall as a mountain. Then it hit them, and suddenly the afternoon turned orange, then almost black. Father switched on the lights and drove slowly, while strong gusts of wind shook the car and sand hissed against the glass.

After half an hour, the wind became weaker and the sky slowly cleared. The family waited at a petrol station until the roads were safe, and then drove home. The next morning, Father and Grandfather went back to the camping place. The tent had been blown away, and the fireplace was completely buried under the sand. "I'm sorry I laughed at your machine," Saad told Faisal quietly.

That evening, Grandfather climbed the stairs to the roof for the first time in years. "When I was young, I read the sky with my eyes," he said, "but you read it with numbers too." Faisal smiled and showed him how the barometer worked, and Grandfather taught him the names of the winds that his own father had taught him. From that day, the blue notebook had two kinds of notes: Faisal's numbers and Grandfather's stories about the sky.

questions.q: What first told Faisal that the weather was going to change?
options: The weather forecast on his tablet
His barometer showed the pressure falling fast
Grandfather saw dark clouds

questions.q: Why did Saad laugh at Faisal?
options: Because there were no clouds in the sky
Because Faisal fell over while playing football
Because Faisal's notebook was blue

questions.q: In the story, the 'horizon' is...
options: a kind of strong wind
a tool for measuring the weather
the line where the land seems to meet the sky

questions.q: What happened to the family's tent?
options: It was buried under the fire
The wind blew it away
Father packed it into the car

questions.q: Why do you think Grandfather climbed to the roof at the end of the story?
options: He wanted to show respect for Faisal and learn about his weather station
He wanted to look for another sandstorm
He wanted to water his daughter-in-law's plants

pages.text: Faris Al-Harbi had a secret that nobody at school knew. He loved art more than any other subject, and his notebooks were full of sketches of old buildings and fishing boats. But when he looked at a red apple and a green leaf, they seemed almost the same colour to him. He was colour-blind, and he was afraid that people would laugh if they found out.

One Sunday morning, Mr Saeed, the art teacher, made an announcement. "Our school is going to paint a huge mural on the wall by the gate," he said. "The theme is 'Our City', and the best design will be chosen by a team of judges next Thursday." The students cheered, and Faris felt his heart beat faster. Then he remembered the colours, and his excitement quickly turned into worry.

That evening, he visited his grandfather in Al-Balad, the old part of Jeddah. Grandfather had spent forty years carving wooden windows called rawasheen for the tall coral houses. "Why the long face?" he asked, putting down his tools. Faris took a deep breath and told him everything about the competition and his problem with colours.

Grandfather smiled and led him to an old window at the top of the stairs. "Look carefully," he said. Sunlight was shining through the carved wood, and it drew beautiful patterns of light and shadow across the floor. "I have never needed a single colour to make something beautiful," Grandfather explained. "Light, shadow and shape can tell a story too."

For the next four days, Faris worked on his design every afternoon. He used blues and yellows, which he could see clearly, and many dark and light shades. His picture showed the old houses of Al-Balad, with the shadows of the rawasheen falling across a quiet street. His best friend Omar looked at it and said, "It looks like the sun is really shining on the paper!"

On Thursday, all the designs were hung in the school hall. Most students had used every colour in the box: bright red cars, green palm trees and orange sunsets. Faris's picture looked very different, and some boys whispered that he had forgotten his colours. He wanted to hide, but instead he stepped forward bravely when the judges reached his work.

"Why did you choose only two colours?" asked one of the judges, a well-known artist from the city. Faris's voice shook a little as he answered. "I'm colour-blind, so I can't see reds and greens well. My grandfather taught me that light and shadow can be just as powerful as colour." The hall went completely silent, and then the artist began to nod slowly.

Faris's design won first prize, and the judges said it was the most original picture they had seen that year. A month later, the mural was finished, and every morning its painted shadows welcomed the students at the gate. Grandfather came to see it, leaning on his stick and smiling proudly. "You see," he said, "you didn't lose any colours. You found a new way of seeing."

questions.q: What was Faris's secret?
options: He was colour-blind.
He did not like art.
He had broken his grandfather's window.

questions.q: What was the theme of the school mural?
options: The Sea
Our City
My Family

questions.q: In the story, what does "original" mean?
options: very old
new and different from others
very colourful

questions.q: How did Grandfather help Faris?
options: He painted the design for him.
He showed him how light and shadow can make something beautiful.
He spoke to the judges before the competition.

questions.q: Why did the hall go silent after Faris spoke?
options: Everyone was surprised and moved by his honest answer.
The judges were angry with him.
The students wanted to go home.

pages.text: Every summer, Yousef stayed at his grandfather's old house in Al-Balad, the historic heart of Jeddah. One hot afternoon, while he was looking for a fan in the storeroom, he found a dusty wooden box. Inside, there was an old camera with a leather strap. A tiny number on the top showed that only two photos were left.

Yousef pointed the camera at the window and pressed the button. There was a bright white flash, and the room seemed to spin around him. When he opened his eyes, he was standing in a narrow street full of tall houses with carved wooden balconies. There were no cars, no phones and no air conditioners, only the smell of the sea and the shouts of men selling fish.

Suddenly, a boy about his age came running round the corner and crashed into him. An envelope fell from the boy's hand, and Yousef picked it up. "Thank you!" the boy said, out of breath. "I'm Saleh. My father's letter must reach Captain Hamid before his ship leaves at noon, but I'm new in Jeddah and I've taken a wrong turn."

Yousef's heart was beating fast, but he wanted to help. His grandfather had told him many stories about these streets, and he recognised the tall white tower of a famous old house. "The port is this way," he said confidently. "If we hurry, we can still make it!"

The two boys ran past busy shops and through a crowded market until they could see the blue water. A large ship was already pulling up its heavy anchor. "Captain Hamid!" Saleh shouted, waving the envelope above his head. A tall man with a grey beard turned, smiled and took the letter just before the ship began to move.

"You saved my family's shop," Saleh said. "That letter was a big order, and without it, my father would have lost everything. What's your name?" Yousef smiled and said, "Just call me a friend." Saleh looked down and laughed, "Your shoes are very strange, friend!" Yousef held the camera at arm's length, took a photo of them together, and the white flash filled the air again.

Yousef was back in the dusty storeroom, holding the camera. At that moment, his grandfather walked in and went completely silent when he saw it. "When I was your age," he said slowly, "a boy with strange shoes and a camera exactly like this one helped me deliver an important letter. I never saw him again, so years later I bought this camera to remember him." Then he looked carefully at Yousef's shoes, and his eyes grew wide.

The next day, they took the film to a small photo shop, and the owner printed the last picture. It showed two smiling boys standing by the sea, with a ship sailing away behind them. Grandfather Saleh held the photo with shaking hands. "I have waited fifty years to say thank you," he said softly, and Yousef hugged him tightly. "You're welcome, my friend," he answered.

questions.q: Where did Yousef find the old camera?
options: In a dusty box in the storeroom
In a small photo shop
On a ship at the port

questions.q: Why was Saleh running through the streets?
options: He was late for school
He had to take a letter to Captain Hamid before noon
He was trying to catch a thief

questions.q: In the story, what does "out of breath" mean?
options: Very angry
Breathing hard after running
Feeling sleepy

questions.q: How did Yousef know the way to the port?
options: He used a map on his phone
A fisherman showed him
He remembered his grandfather's stories and recognised a famous tower

questions.q: Why did Grandfather look carefully at Yousef's shoes?
options: He realised that Yousef was the boy who helped him long ago
He thought the shoes were dirty
He wanted to buy the same shoes

pages.text: Every Friday morning, Faisal went fishing with his grandfather on the Red Sea coast near Yanbu. They always took their small boat past the mangroves, strange trees that grow in salty water with their roots standing up like fingers. "These trees are older than me," Grandfather said. "They protect the coast from storms, and baby fish hide between their roots." Faisal nodded, but secretly he thought they were just ugly bushes.

One Friday, Grandfather turned off the engine and frowned. The water near the trees was full of rubbish: plastic bottles, bags, and an old fishing net caught in the roots. Suddenly, something moved under the net. Faisal leaned over the side of the boat. "Grandfather, look! It's a turtle!" he shouted.

The turtle was trapped, and one of its front legs was wrapped tightly in the net. It was trying to swim, but it was getting tired. Grandfather handed Faisal a small knife. "Cut carefully, close to the net, not near the leg," he said calmly. Faisal's hands were shaking, but he held the net still and began to cut.

After a few long minutes, the last piece of net fell away. The turtle rested for a moment, then pushed its strong legs against the water and disappeared into the blue. Faisal laughed with relief, but Grandfather looked sadly at the rubbish around them. "When I was your age, this water was so clear that you could see every fish," he said. "Now people throw everything away and forget that the sea remembers."

That night, Faisal couldn't sleep. He searched online and discovered that mangroves store more carbon than many forests on land, and that they were disappearing in many countries. He also found photos of turtles that had not been as lucky as his. In the morning, he took his laptop to school and showed his science teacher, Mr. Khalid.

"If we do nothing, more animals will get hurt," Faisal explained to his class. Mr. Khalid suggested a clean-up day, and soon thirty students had signed up. Some parents offered boats, and a local fishermen's group promised to collect the old nets. Even Faisal's little sister, Noura, made posters that said, "The sea is not a bin!"

On Saturday, the beach was busy with families wearing gloves and carrying bags. They worked all morning in the hot sun, pulling plastic out of the roots and the sand. By lunchtime, they had filled more than two hundred bags. A reporter from the local newspaper took photos and asked Faisal why he had organised the event. "Because these trees look after the sea," he said, "so we have to look after them."

A few weeks later, Faisal and Grandfather took the boat out again. The water between the mangroves was clean, and tiny silver fish were swimming between the roots. Then a familiar shape rose to the surface, with a small scar on its front leg. Faisal smiled and waved as the turtle swam past. "You know," he told his grandfather, "I think these trees are actually quite beautiful."

questions.q: Where did Faisal and his grandfather go fishing?
options: On the Red Sea coast near Yanbu
On a lake near Riyadh
On the Gulf coast near Dammam

questions.q: What did Faisal secretly think about the mangroves at the beginning?
options: They were the most beautiful trees in the world
They were just ugly bushes
They were dangerous for fish

questions.q: "Faisal laughed with relief." What does "relief" mean here?
options: A feeling of anger after a problem
A feeling of fear before something bad happens
A happy feeling when a worry or danger has ended

questions.q: Why did Faisal show his laptop to Mr. Khalid?
options: He wanted to share what he had learned about mangroves and turtles
He needed help with his maths homework
He wanted to show photos of his fishing trip

questions.q: How did Faisal probably know it was the same turtle at the end?
options: It swam very fast
It had a small scar on its front leg
It was much bigger than other turtles

stories.title: The Night Fixer of Al-Ward Street

pages.text: When Rakan's family moved to Abha, nothing seemed to go right for him. On his first week, his bicycle got a flat tyre, and he had no money to repair it. He left it next to the wall of their building and went to bed in a bad mood. The next morning, he couldn't believe his eyes: the tyre was full of air and the chain was shining.

"Did Dad fix it?" Rakan asked his older sister, Jana. "No, he left for work before sunrise," she replied. Over the next few days, more strange things happened on Al-Ward Street. The broken bench near the mosque was painted green, and the noisy gate of the school stopped making its terrible sound.

"Someone is fixing our street at night," Jana said, her eyes wide. "Let's find out who it is!" They made a plan to stay awake on Thursday night and watch from their window. Rakan took a notebook to write down everything they saw, like a real detective.

Just after midnight, a thin shadow appeared under the streetlight. It was an old man carrying a heavy toolbox, and he was walking slowly towards the water pipe that had been leaking for weeks. Rakan whispered, "That's Uncle Idris from the ground floor! He never talks to anyone." They watched quietly as he worked carefully until the water stopped dripping.

In the morning, they told their father about it. He smiled sadly and explained that Uncle Idris had been a mechanic for forty years. "Since his wife passed away, he has been living alone, and I think he finds it hard to sleep," he said. Jana looked at her brother and said, "He has been kind to everyone, but has anyone been kind to him?"

That afternoon, the two of them wrote a letter that said, "Thank you, Night Fixer. We know your secret!" They put it in an envelope with a small box of their mother's date biscuits. Rakan knocked on the old man's door, then both of them ran away, laughing nervously. From behind a car, they saw Uncle Idris open the door, read the letter, and touch his eyes.

The next Friday, their father invited Uncle Idris to lunch after the prayer. At first he was shy, but soon he was telling funny stories about the old cars he had repaired. "I thought nobody noticed what I did," he admitted quietly. "Of course we noticed," Rakan said. "Our street is better because of you."

Now, every Saturday morning, Rakan and Jana help Uncle Idris with his repairs, and he teaches them how to use his tools. He doesn't have to work in the dark anymore, because he isn't alone. Sometimes neighbours bring him tea or ask for his advice, and he always smiles. Rakan has learned that kindness is like a good tool: the more you use it, the more useful it becomes.

questions.q: What was the first strange thing that happened to Rakan?
options: His bicycle was fixed during the night.
His school gate was painted green.
He found a letter at his door.

questions.q: Why did Rakan and Jana stay awake on Thursday night?
options: They wanted to finish their homework.
They wanted to find out who was fixing the street.
They were waiting for their father to come home.

questions.q: In the story, the pipe was "leaking." What does this mean?
options: It was very old and dirty.
It was making a loud noise.
Water was coming out of it where it shouldn't.

questions.q: Why did Uncle Idris touch his eyes after reading the letter?
options: He had something in his eye from the work.
He was moved and happy that someone thanked him.
He couldn't read the letter without glasses.

questions.q: What is the main message of the story?
options: Kindness should be returned and shared with others.
It is dangerous to go outside at night.
Old people should not work with tools.

pages.text: Faisal had always thought the desert was empty. That changed on the first night of the winter holiday, when Uncle Khalid drove him and his sister Noura deep into the Nafud to join the family camp. "Grandfather is already there," Uncle Khalid said, smiling. "He's making his famous coffee."

An hour later, the sun was going down, and the red dunes looked like waves of fire. Suddenly the car shook and stopped, and the back wheels were stuck deep in the soft sand. Uncle Khalid jumped out to look, but he stepped on a rock and twisted his ankle. "Don't worry," he said, although his face showed pain.

Faisal checked his phone, but there was no signal at all. The car's map screen showed only a blue dot in the middle of nowhere. "The camp is about three kilometres north of here," Uncle Khalid said. "I can't walk that far with this foot." Noura looked at Faisal, and he knew exactly what she was thinking.

"We can go and bring help," Noura said. Uncle Khalid was worried at first, but finally he agreed, because it was getting cold quickly. He gave them a torch, a bottle of water and his thick jacket. "Stay together, and if you get lost, come straight back to the car lights," he told them.

The children climbed the first dune, but when they reached the top, every direction looked the same. The sky had turned dark, and thousands of stars appeared above them. Faisal suddenly remembered something Grandfather had taught him last summer. "Look for the star that never moves," Grandfather had said. "Our grandparents used it to find their way for hundreds of years."

Faisal searched the sky until he found a shape like a big spoon. He followed its two front stars upwards to a small, bright star standing alone. "That's Al-Jadi, the North Star!" he shouted. "If we walk towards it, we'll reach the camp." They started walking, checking the star every few minutes so they would not lose their way.

The walk was harder than they had expected, because their feet sank into the sand with every step. When Noura began to feel tired, Faisal held her hand and told her stories to keep her going. After almost an hour, they heard a sound in the distance. It was the soft music of an oud, and then they saw the orange light of a fire.

Grandfather stood up in surprise when the two children walked out of the darkness. Soon the uncles drove out with ropes and found Uncle Khalid, who was cold but safe. Later, sitting by the fire with a cup of warm milk, Faisal looked up at Al-Jadi again. "You remembered," Grandfather said proudly. Faisal smiled, because now he understood that the desert was never empty: it was full of stars, stories and paths for anyone who knew how to read them.

questions.q: Why did the car stop in the desert?
options: It ran out of petrol.
Its back wheels were stuck in soft sand.
Uncle Khalid hit a big rock.

questions.q: Why couldn't Uncle Khalid walk to the camp?
options: He had twisted his ankle.
He was too tired after driving.
He had to look after the car.

questions.q: In the story, the word "signal" is closest in meaning to:
options: a light from a fire
a connection for a phone
a type of map

questions.q: How did Faisal know which way to walk?
options: He used the map on his phone.
He followed car tracks in the sand.
He followed the North Star, as Grandfather had taught him.

questions.q: What can we understand about Faisal at the end of the story?
options: He now sees the desert in a new and richer way.
He never wants to visit the desert again.
He thinks phones are more useful than stars.

stories.title: The Night of the Tiny Travellers

pages.text: Every August, Lina and her younger brother Faisal spent a week at their grandfather's house on the Red Sea coast, not far from Umluj. Grandfather Saeed had been a fisherman for forty years, and he knew the sea better than anyone. Lina loved his stories, but this summer he had promised them something better than a story. "This year," he said with a smile, "you will see a secret with your own eyes."

On the first morning, he led them along the beach to a small circle of white stones. "Two months ago, a green turtle came out of the sea here at night," he explained. "She dug a deep hole, laid about a hundred eggs, and then went back to the water." Faisal stared at the sand. "Are they still down there?" he whispered. "Yes," said Grandfather, "and I think they will hatch very soon, maybe even tonight."

After dinner, the family walked quietly back to the nest. "No torches and no phones," Grandfather warned. "Baby turtles find the sea by following the brightest light, and that should be the moon shining on the water." But Lina noticed something worrying further down the beach. A new café had opened there, and its strong white lights were shining across the sand like a football stadium.

Just before midnight, the sand inside the circle began to move. First one tiny head appeared, then another, and suddenly dozens of baby turtles were climbing out, each one no bigger than Lina's hand. "They're amazing!" Faisal breathed. Then Lina's smile disappeared. Instead of heading towards the waves, the turtles were turning the wrong way, towards the café and the busy road behind it.

"Stay with Grandfather!" Lina told Faisal, and she ran across the sand as fast as she could. At the café, the owner was carrying a tray of tea to his customers. Out of breath, Lina explained about the turtles and the lights. The man frowned. "If I switch them off, my customers won't be able to see anything," he said. "Please," Lina begged. "If you don't, they'll die on the road before they ever reach the sea."

For a moment, the owner said nothing. Then an old man at one of the tables stood up. "My son, the girl is right," he said calmly. "We can drink our tea in the dark for a few minutes." The owner nodded, walked to the wall and pressed a switch, and the whole beach went dark.

Slowly, Lina's eyes got used to the darkness, and she saw the silver path of the moon on the sea. One by one, the little turtles stopped, turned around and began hurrying towards the water. Faisal and Grandfather walked beside them, making sure that crabs and birds stayed away. When the last turtle disappeared into the waves, Faisal said proudly, "I counted eighty-seven!" Behind them, the café customers began to clap.

The next evening, the family went back to the café and found a surprise. The owner had replaced the bright white lights with soft orange ones that pointed away from the beach, and a new sign said: "Turtle nesting area – please keep the beach dark." "Only one baby turtle in a thousand grows up," Grandfather told the children, "but the females return to the beach where they were born." Lina looked out at the moonlit sea and smiled, imagining a big green turtle climbing onto this same sand, many years from now.

questions.q: Why did Grandfather put white stones on the beach?
options: To show where the turtle eggs were
To help fishermen find the café
To build a wall against the waves

questions.q: Why were the baby turtles going the wrong way?
options: They were afraid of the crabs
They were following the café's bright lights
Faisal was using a torch

questions.q: In the story, "Lina begged" the owner. What does "begged" mean?
options: Shouted angrily
Asked very strongly and seriously
Asked without caring

questions.q: What helped the café owner decide to switch off the lights?
options: Grandfather paid him money
The police told him to do it
An old customer agreed with Lina

questions.q: What can we understand about the café owner at the end of the story?
options: He wanted to protect the turtles in the future
He was still angry with Lina
He decided to close his café

pages.text: Faisal was twelve, and he was the youngest member of his school's radio club in Riyadh. One Sunday morning, Mr. Khalid, their teacher, walked into the room with a huge smile. "Our school has been chosen," he said. "Next Thursday, we are going to talk to an astronaut on the International Space Station!" Each student could ask one question, and Faisal already knew what his would be.

Mr. Khalid explained that the space station travels at about 28,000 kilometres per hour. "It will appear over the horizon at 8:14 in the evening," he said. "After ten minutes, it will disappear again, so we can't waste a single second." Faisal wrote his question on a small card and practised it every night: "What does Earth look like at night from space?"

On Thursday afternoon, the sky suddenly turned orange. A strong dust storm swept across the city, and the wind shook the windows of the school. By the time it had finished, the families were already arriving in the hall for the big event. Then Mr. Khalid came back from the roof, and his face was pale. "The antenna is bent," he said quietly. "Without it, we won't hear anything."

Faisal remembered the summer he had spent helping his grandfather repair an old radio in the village. "Sir, can I help?" he asked. Mr. Khalid hesitated, then nodded, and together they climbed the stairs to the roof. Dust was still blowing in the air, so they covered their faces and worked quickly. Using strong tape and a metal pole from the storeroom, they managed to make the antenna stand straight again.

At 8:14, everyone in the hall held their breath, but the speaker made only a soft hissing noise. A minute passed, and still there was nothing. Faisal looked at the map on the wall and suddenly realised the problem. "The station is coming from the north-west, but the storm turned the antenna to the east!" He and Mr. Khalid ran back upstairs and turned it as fast as they could.

When they returned, a clear, friendly voice was filling the hall. "Hello, Riyadh! This is the International Space Station. Can you hear me?" The students cheered, and then, one by one, they stepped up to the microphone. They asked how astronauts sleep, what food they eat, and whether they ever feel homesick.

At 8:22, the signal was getting weaker, and Faisal was the last in line. His hands were shaking as he read his card. There was a long crackle, and he thought he had been too late. Then the astronaut answered, "Right now, I can see the lights of your city shining like gold, and a long cloud of dust beside them. Thank you for not giving up tonight."

A moment later, the voice disappeared, and the whole hall stood up and clapped. Later that night, Faisal and his father went up to the roof of their house. pages.text: Faisal had been captain of the Al-Nakheel Junior team for two seasons, and he was proud of his loud voice. "Pass! Man on! Shoot!" he shouted at every training session, and everyone listened. One Sunday afternoon, Coach Saleh walked onto the pitch with a tall, thin boy carrying a blue bag. "This is Omar," the coach said. "He's just moved here from Abha, and he's going to play with us."

Omar was fast, and he could control the ball as if it was glued to his feet. But during the practice match, something strange happened. Faisal shouted "Behind you!" three times, and Omar didn't turn around. A defender took the ball easily, and Faisal threw his arms in the air. "Why don't you listen?" he said angrily.

After training, Coach Saleh took Faisal aside. "Omar can't hear, Faisal," he explained quietly. "He was born deaf, but he reads lips and uses sign language." Faisal's face went hot with shame. He had been angry with a boy for something that wasn't his fault.

The next day, Faisal waited for Omar by the school gate and said sorry slowly, so Omar could read his lips. Omar smiled and typed a message on his phone: "No problem, but shouting doesn't help me. Maybe we need a new language." That evening, the two boys sat on the roof of Faisal's house and invented signals for the team. A closed fist meant "defend", a pointing finger meant "pass to me", and a hand on the head meant "far post".

At first, some of the players laughed and said the signs were silly. "Real footballers shout," said Hamad, the goalkeeper. But after two weeks of practice, the team was playing better than ever. They didn't waste their breath, and the other teams never knew what they were planning.

The final of the city cup was played in a big stadium, and thousands of families had come to watch. The noise was unbelievable, with drums, horns and cheering from every side. Faisal tried to shout to his defenders, but even he couldn't hear his own voice. The score was 1-1, and there were only two minutes left.

Then the referee blew his whistle: a free kick for Al-Nakheel, just outside the box. Faisal stood over the ball and looked across at Omar, who was waiting near the defenders. Without a word, Faisal put his hand on his head. Omar nodded and moved quietly towards the far post, while the defenders watched the wrong players.

Faisal curled the ball high over the wall, and Omar met it with a perfect header. The net shook, and the stadium exploded with noise. Omar couldn't hear the crowd, but he could see his whole team running towards him, making a new sign with their hands: the one for "thank you". Later, holding the cup, Faisal smiled. He had always believed that a captain needed a loud voice, but now he knew that the best leaders also know how to listen.

Looking after a pet is a big responsibility.
Teenagers want to be more independent.
My parents are quite strict about bedtime.
My curfew is eight o'clock on school nights.

dialogue.t: Do you think teenagers have enough freedom?
Not really. I think teenagers should be allowed to go to the shops alone.
I agree. It helps us become more independent. However, I think we should tell our parents where we are.
Of course. What about phones? Should we be allowed to use them at night?
Hmm, I think teenagers should be allowed to use them until nine. However, after that we need to sleep.
That's fair. My parents are quite strict, so my curfew for my phone is eight.
Well, freedom comes with responsibility. If we show we're responsible, they might give us more.

grammar.title: should be allowed to + However
grammar.ar: نستخدم should be allowed to + الفعل في صيغته الأساسية لنقول إنه من الصواب أن يُسمح لشخص بفعل شيء. الفعل بعد to يبقى دون أي إضافات. ونستخدم However في بداية جملة جديدة لنعبّر عن فكرة معاكسة، ونضع بعدها فاصلة.
examples: I think teenagers should be allowed to choose their own clothes.
Students should be allowed to bring snacks to class. However, they must keep the room clean.
Children shouldn't be allowed to play video games all day.

words.ex: My grandmother is elderly, but she still walks every day.
Some old people feel lonely because they live alone.
My mum takes care of my grandfather when he is ill.
I often keep my grandma company in the evenings.
You need to be patient when you teach someone to use a phone.
In our culture, we show respect to older people.

dialogue.t: My grandfather lives alone now, and I think he feels lonely.
That's sad. If we visit them more often, they will feel happier.
You're right. I could keep him company after school on Thursdays.
Good idea. You could also teach him to make video calls.
Yes! If he learns how to use his phone, he will talk to the family every day.
But you need to be patient. Unless we explain things slowly, he won't understand.
True. And unless we help him with the shopping, he will have to carry heavy bags.
Let's make a plan to take care of him together.

grammar.title: First conditional with if and unless
grammar.ar: نستخدم الجملة الشرطية الأولى للحديث عن نتيجة محتملة في المستقبل: If + المضارع البسيط، ثم will + الفعل الأساسي. كلمة unless تعني «إلّا إذا» أو «إذا لم»، فجملة Unless we visit them تعني If we don't visit them. لا نستخدم will بعد if أو unless مباشرة.
examples: If we visit them more often, they will feel less lonely.
Unless we help them, they won't be able to carry their shopping.
If you listen to your grandparents' stories, you will learn a lot.

words.ex: One advantage of social media is sharing news quickly.
A big disadvantage is that it wastes a lot of time.
I keep in touch with my cousins in Jordan online.
Some apps are very addictive, so it's hard to stop.
Check your privacy settings so strangers can't see your photos.
Think carefully before you post a photo online.

dialogue.t: Our teacher asked us to discuss social media. What do you think?
On the one hand, it helps us keep in touch with friends and family abroad.
Yes, and you can learn new things from videos. On the other hand, it can be really addictive.
Exactly. Some people spend five hours a day scrolling!
There's also the problem of privacy. People post personal photos without thinking.
That's true. So overall, I think social media is useful if we use it carefully.
I agree. Overall, I think we need clear time limits.

grammar.title: Linking ideas: On the one hand / On the other hand / Overall
grammar.ar: نستخدم On the one hand لعرض الجانب الأول من الموضوع، وOn the other hand لعرض الجانب المقابل. ثم نستخدم Overall, I think لتلخيص رأينا النهائي. نضع فاصلة بعد كل عبارة من هذه العبارات.
examples: On the one hand, social media helps us share ideas.
On the other hand, it can make people feel bad about themselves.
Overall, I think the advantages are bigger than the disadvantages.

words.ex: It's hard to trust someone you've never met.
Never send your photos to strangers online.
Don't share personal information like your address.
I'd like to meet my online friend in person one day.
Everyone has a different point of view on this topic.
I partly agree with you, but not completely.

dialogue.t: I think online friends can be just as good as real friends.
I see your point, but you can't be sure who they really are.
That's true for strangers. But I only chat with people from my gaming club.
I partly agree because clubs are safer. However, you still shouldn't share personal information.
Of course, I never do that. My online friends help me when I'm sad.
I see your point, but a friend in person can give you a hug!
Ha! Fair enough. Maybe we need both kinds of friends.
Now that's a point of view I completely agree with!

grammar.title: Agreeing and disagreeing politely
grammar.ar: من الأدب في الإنجليزية ألّا نقول You're wrong مباشرة. نبدأ بإظهار الاحترام لرأي الآخر بقول I see your point, but... ثم نذكر رأينا المختلف. ونقول I partly agree because... عندما نتفق مع جزء من الفكرة فقط.
examples: I see your point, but online friends can't help you in real life.
I partly agree because some websites are safe.
I see your point, but I think we should be careful.

words.ex: There aren't many trees in my neighbourhood.
We want to improve the park near our school.
We need more recycling bins on our street.
Our posters will raise awareness about saving water.
Our project has a small budget of 200 dinars.
We wrote a letter to the local council about the broken lights.

dialogue.t: Good morning, everyone. Our idea is to turn the empty land near our school into a small garden.
At the moment, it's full of rubbish, and nobody uses it.
This would help the environment because we would plant trees and flowers.
It would also give elderly people a quiet place to sit and children a safe place to play.
We need permission from the local council and a small budget for plants and benches.
We also need volunteers to water the plants every week.
Finally, we'd put recycling bins there to raise awareness about rubbish.
Thank you for listening. Do you have any questions?

grammar.title: Presenting a plan: Our idea is to / would / need
grammar.ar: نستخدم Our idea is to + الفعل الأساسي لتقديم فكرة المشروع. ونستخدم would + الفعل الأساسي للحديث عن نتيجة متخيَّلة لمشروع لم يحدث بعد، مثل: This would help. ونستخدم need + اسم أو need + to + فعل لذكر ما نحتاجه لتنفيذ المشروع.
examples: Our idea is to paint the old walls in our street.
This would help people feel proud of their neighbourhood.
We need paint, brushes and ten volunteers.

words.ex: Cars and factories produce greenhouse gases every day.
Oil, gas and coal are fossil fuels.
Global warming is making summers hotter in many countries.
Scientists say the sea level is rising slowly.
The drought lasted two years, so farmers lost their crops.
Cutting down forests can lead to floods.

dialogue.t: Our science teacher talked about climate change today. Do you know what causes it?
Yes. Burning fossil fuels causes greenhouse gases, which leads to global warming.
And what happens when the Earth gets warmer?
The ice at the poles melts. As a result, the sea level rises.
That sounds dangerous for cities near the sea.
It is. Hotter weather also causes droughts, which leads to less food and water.
So we should use less energy at home.
Exactly. Even small changes can help.

grammar.title: Linking causes and effects
grammar.ar: نستخدم الفعل causes بمعنى (يُسبِّب) لنربط السبب بنتيجته، مثل: Pollution causes disease. ونستخدم which leads to بمعنى (مما يؤدي إلى) لنضيف نتيجة جديدة في نفس الجملة، وتأتي بعدها كلمة أو اسم. أما As a result فتعني (نتيجةً لذلك)، ونضعها في بداية جملة جديدة وبعدها فاصلة.
examples: Too much traffic causes air pollution.
People cut down trees, which leads to fewer homes for animals.
It didn't rain for months. As a result, the rivers became dry.

words.ex: The Saudi Green Initiative wants to make the country greener.
Sun and wind give us renewable energy.
There are solar panels on the roof of our school.
Trees help reduce heat in the city.
New nature reserves protect animals like the Arabian oryx.
The country plans to cut its carbon emissions.

dialogue.t: Have you heard about the Saudi Green Initiative?
Yes! Millions of trees are being planted across the country.
Why are they planting so many trees?
The project is designed to reduce heat and make the air cleaner.
I also read about Green Riyadh. Parks are being built all over the city.
That's great. And huge solar farms are being built in the desert, too.
What are they for?
They are designed to produce renewable energy from the sun.

grammar.title: Present continuous passive and 'designed to'
grammar.ar: نستخدم المبني للمجهول في المضارع المستمر (is / are + being + التصريف الثالث للفعل) عندما نتحدث عن عمل يحدث الآن ويكون الفعل نفسه أهم من الشخص الذي يقوم به، مثل: Trees are being planted. ونستخدم is designed to + الفعل الأساسي لنشرح الهدف من مشروع أو شيء ما، وتعني (صُمِّم من أجل أن).
examples: Millions of trees are being planted in Saudi Arabia.
A new park is being built near my house.
This project is designed to protect wildlife.

words.ex: Our family produces a lot of waste every week.
Single-use plastic bags are bad for the sea.
I bring a reusable bottle to school every day.
We recycle paper and cans at home.
This toy has too much plastic packaging.
Most plastic ends up in a landfill or in the ocean.

dialogue.t: Look at this bin. There is too much plastic in it!
I know. We use too many plastic bottles at school.
And a lot of them end up in the sea.
Instead, we could bring reusable bottles from home.
Good idea. There is also too much packaging on our snacks.
Instead, we could buy fruit, which doesn't need any plastic.
Let's ask our teacher to put a recycling bin in the classroom.
Great! I'll make a poster for it.

grammar.title: Too much / too many and suggesting with 'could'
grammar.ar: نستخدم too much مع الأسماء غير المعدودة مثل plastic وwaste وwater، ونستخدم too many مع الأسماء المعدودة بصيغة الجمع مثل bottles وbags، وكلاهما يعني (كثير جداً أكثر من اللازم). ولاقتراح حل نقول Instead, we could + الفعل الأساسي، وتعني (بدلاً من ذلك، يمكننا أن).
examples: There is too much rubbish on the beach.
We use too many plastic bags when we go shopping.
Instead, we could use cloth bags.

words.ex: In a smart city, traffic lights can change by themselves.
Good public transport means fewer cars on the road.
Future cities might have green skyscrapers covered in plants.
My uncle has just bought an electric car.
The population of Riyadh is growing very fast.
Pollution makes it hard to breathe in big cities.

dialogue.t: What do you think cities will be like in 2050?
In 2050 cities will be much greener, with gardens on every building.
I agree. People might travel in flying taxis!
Maybe! I think there won't be any petrol cars. Everything will be electric.
So there won't be so much pollution.
Exactly. And robots might deliver our shopping.
Do you think people will still go to school?
Yes, but students might learn with virtual reality.

grammar.title: Future predictions: will, might, won't
grammar.ar: نستخدم will + الفعل الأساسي للتنبؤ بشيء نحن متأكدون منه في المستقبل، ونستخدم won't (أي will not) للنفي. أما might + الفعل الأساسي فنستخدمها عندما يكون الأمر ممكناً لكننا غير متأكدين، وتعني (قد / ربما). لاحظ أن الفعل بعدها لا يأخذ s أو ing.
examples: In 2050 cities will be cleaner and quieter.
People might live in tall green towers.
There won't be any traffic jams.

words.ex: We were stuck in a traffic jam for an hour.
Big cars use a lot of fuel.
A car is convenient because you can leave any time.
The train was crowded in the morning.
I take the metro to visit my cousins in Riyadh.
Trains are more environmentally friendly than planes.

dialogue.t: Which is better for a city: cars or trains?
I strongly believe trains are better. One reason is that they carry hundreds of people at once.
But cars are more convenient. You can go anywhere, anytime.
That's true, but another reason is that trains cause less pollution.
Hmm. Trains can be crowded, though.
Yes, but cars cause traffic jams. On the metro, you never get stuck in traffic.
I strongly believe we need both. Some places don't have stations.
OK, that's a fair point.

grammar.title: Giving opinions and reasons
grammar.ar: عندما نناقش موضوعاً نبدأ برأينا بعبارة I strongly believe (that) وتعني (أؤمن بشدة أن)، ثم نقدم الأسباب بشكل مرتب: One reason is (that) أي (أحد الأسباب هو أن)، ثم Another reason is (that) أي (سبب آخر هو أن). هذا الترتيب يجعل كلامنا واضحاً ومقنعاً في النقاش.
examples: I strongly believe that buses are better than cars.
One reason is that they are cheaper.
Another reason is that they are better for the environment.

words.ex: The audience clapped at the end of my speech.
I want to persuade my friends to recycle.
We must take action before it's too late.
Our posters will raise awareness about saving water.
We need to protect the planet for future generations.
Even one person can make a difference.

dialogue.t: Can you listen to my speech? I want to practise it.
Sure, go ahead.
Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about saving water.
Saudi Arabia is a dry country, so every drop is important. We must turn off the tap when we brush our teeth.
We mustn't waste water in our gardens. Together we can make a difference. Thank you for listening.
That was great! Your message was very clear.
Thanks! Was it persuasive enough?
Yes, but try to look at the audience more and speak a bit slower.

grammar.title: Using must and mustn't to persuade
grammar.ar: نستخدم must + الفعل الأساسي للتعبير عن شيء ضروري ومهم جداً، وتعني (يجب). ونستخدم mustn't (أي must not) لنقول إن شيئاً ممنوع أو خطأ، وتعني (يجب ألا). في الخطاب الإقناعي نستخدم We must لنشجع الجمهور على التحرك معاً، ونبدأ الخطاب بـ Today I want to talk about ونختمه بـ Thank you for listening.
examples: Today I want to talk about plastic in our oceans.
We must recycle our bottles and cans.
We mustn't throw rubbish on the beach.
